name: A throughput number without batch size, concurrency, input/output length, and warmup is meaningless
symptom: A vendor claims '1000 tokens/sec' but doesn't specify whether that's at batch 1 or batch 128, with 128-token or 8192-token inputs, with or without warmup. The actual serving throughput at your workload could be 10x lower.
root_cause: Throughput is a function of: batch size (larger = higher throughput but higher latency), input length (longer = more prefill work), output length (longer = more decode steps), concurrency (more requests = better GPU utilization), and warmup (JIT compilation, cache warming). Omitting any of these makes the number uninterpretable.
workaround: Always require: (1) batch size or concurrency level, (2) input token length, (3) output token length, (4) warmup procedure (e.g., '100 warmup iterations'), (5) whether the number is per-request or aggregate. Compare only numbers measured at the same operating point.
notes: This is the most common performance marketing trick. A '1000 tokens/sec' claim at batch 128 with 8192-token inputs might be 50 tokens/sec at batch 1 with 128-token inputs. The repo's benchmark schema requires methodology for exactly this reason.
